nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the adventure novel and the imperial romance
literary_identity: Novelist, historian and statesman; the author of The Thirty-Nine Steps and the greatest Scottish writer of adventure in the century.
biography: Born in Perth on 26 August 1875, the son of a Free Church minister; he was educated at Glasgow and Oxford, worked in South Africa with Milner, and served as a war correspondent and in intelligence. The Thirty-Nine Steps (1915), Greenmantle (1916), The Three Hostages (1924), Sick Heart River (1941) and the histories followed, and he was Governor-General of Canada from 1935. He died in Montreal on 11 February 1940.
literary_profile: Buchan was the greatest Scottish writer of adventure in the century and the inventor of the modern political thriller: The Thirty-Nine Steps created the chase novel and the man-on-the-run, and Greenmantle and the Richard Hannay books gave the English adventure story its intelligence and its moral seriousness.
stylistic_characteristics: The chase through landscape; the competent amateur hero; the topographical exactness; the political conspiracy at the heart of the ordinary; the plain, rapid, confident narrative.
intellectual_concerns: Empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation.
historical_significance: John Buchan invented the modern political thriller: The Thirty-Nine Steps created the chase novel and the man-on-the-run, and the Hannay books gave the English adventure story its intelligence, its moral seriousness, and a permanent place in the century's fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the essay, the parody and the caricature
literary_identity: Essayist, parodist and caricaturist; the wittiest writer of the 1890s and the finest parodist in English.
biography: Born Henry Maximilian Beerbohm in Kensington on 24 August 1872; he went from Charterhouse to Oxford, published The Works of Max Beerbohm in 1896 and became the drama critic of the Saturday Review in 1898. Zuleika Dobson (1911), Seven Men (1919) and A Christmas Garland (1912), the greatest book of parodies in English, followed. He lived in Rapallo from 1910 and died there on 20 May 1956.
literary_profile: Beerbohm was the wittiest writer of the 1890s and the finest parodist in English: Zuleika Dobson is the only great English comic novel about Oxford, A Christmas Garland ended the art of parody by perfecting it, and his caricatures made him the century's finest comic draughtsman of writers.
stylistic_characteristics: The parody that catches the style exactly; the essay of elegant nonsense; the caricature in prose; the period detail of the 1890s; the epigram and the exquisite, measured sentence.
intellectual_concerns: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist; the jazz age and the pleasure economy; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self.
historical_significance: Max Beerbohm was the wittiest writer of the 1890s and the finest parodist in English: Zuleika Dobson is the only great English comic novel about Oxford, and A Christmas Garland perfected and thereby ended the art of parody.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-French; the comic verse and the polemical essay
literary_identity: Poet, essayist, historian and controversialist; the author of Cautionary Tales and one of the great English comic poets.
biography: Born Joseph Hilaire Pierre Rene Belloc at La Celle-Saint-Cloud near Paris on 27 July 1870, the son of a French barrister and an English mother; he was educated at the Oratory and Balliol, and became a naturalised Briton in 1902. The Bad Child's Book of Beasts (1896), The Path to Rome (1902), Cautionary Tales for Children (1907) and his histories and polemics followed. He died at Guildford on 16 July 1953.
literary_profile: Belloc wrote the funniest children's verse in English and one of the great English travel books: Cautionary Tales made the comic moral poem a permanent form, The Path to Rome invented the modern walking book, and his polemics made him the most pugnacious Catholic man of letters of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic moral tale in regular verse; the absurd catastrophe delivered deadpan; the walking narrative of the pilgrim; the polemical essay of the distributist; the plain, vigorous, opinionated prose.
intellectual_concerns: Religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; childhood, the nursery, and the Edwardian idyll.
historical_significance: Hilaire Belloc wrote the funniest children's verse in English and one of the great English travel books: Cautionary Tales made the comic moral poem a permanent form, and The Path to Rome invented the modern walking book.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the war memoir and the feminist pacifist
literary_identity: Writer, feminist and pacifist; the author of Testament of Youth, the greatest English memoir of the First World War.
biography: Born Vera Mary Brittain at Newcastle-under-Lyme on 29 December 1893; she went up to Somerville College, Oxford, in 1914, served as a VAD nurse in London, Malta and France, and lost her fiance, her brother and two of her closest friends. Testament of Youth (1933), Testament of Friendship (1940), Testament of Experience (1957) and her pacifist journalism followed. She died in Wimbledon on 29 March 1970.
literary_profile: Testament of Youth is the greatest English memoir of the First World War and the central woman's record of the conflict: it made the experience of the war generation of women visible, and it founded the modern literature of grief, pacifism and feminist witness.
stylistic_characteristics: The memoir built from letters and diaries; the plain, exact, unornamented record; the interleaving of private grief and public history; the feminist argument carried by narrative; the elegy for a generation.
intellectual_concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; suffrage, feminism, and the woman's work; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self.
historical_significance: Testament of Youth is the greatest English memoir of the First World War and the central woman's record of the conflict: it made the experience of the war generation of women visible and founded the modern literature of grief, pacifism and feminist witness.

literary_identity: Poet and painter; the author of In Parenthesis, the greatest English poem of the First World War.
biography: Born Walter David Michael Jones at Brockley, Kent, on 1 November 1895 to a Welsh father and an English mother; he served with the Royal Welch Fusiliers on the Somme, at Ypres and at Passchendaele, and converted to Catholicism in 1921. In Parenthesis (1937) and The Anathemata (1952) followed, and he was awarded the Order of the Companions of Honour in 1974. He died in Harrow on 28 October 1974.
literary_profile: In Parenthesis is the greatest English poem of the First World War and one of the central modernist long poems: its combination of prose and verse, its Welsh and Catholic mythology and its exact record of the infantry experience made it a unique achievement, and The Anathemata extended it into a mythic history of Britain.
stylistic_characteristics: The mixed form of prose and verse; the footnote and the annotation; the Welsh, Latin and liturgical allusion woven into the soldiers' speech; the exact topography of the trench; the ritual and liturgical frame.
intellectual_concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination; religion, doubt, and the post-war faith.
historical_significance: In Parenthesis is the greatest English poem of the First World War: its combination of prose and verse, its Welsh and Catholic mythology and its exact record of the infantry experience made it a unique achievement, and it stands with The Waste Land as the central English modernist long poem.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the trench play and the screen
literary_identity: Playwright and screenwriter; the author of Journey's End, the greatest play of the First World War.
biography: Born Robert Cedric Sherriff at Kingston upon Thames on 6 June 1896; he worked in insurance, served as a captain in the East Surrey Regiment on the Western Front, and wrote Journey's End from his own experience; it was produced in 1928 and became the great success of the London stage. Badger's Green (1930), St Helena (1934) and the screenplays for The Invisible Man, Goodbye, Mr Chips and The Dam Busters followed. He died at Kingston on 13 November 1975.
literary_profile: Sherriff wrote Journey's End, the greatest play of the First World War and the central dramatic text of the war: its dugout, its officers and its ordinary courage made the war visible to the theatre audience of 1928 and it remains the most performed war play in English.
stylistic_characteristics: The single dugout set and the unbroken real time; the ordinary speech of the officers; the raid and the waiting; the class hierarchy inside the platoon; the tragic ending without rhetoric.
intellectual_concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent.
historical_significance: R. C. Sherriff wrote Journey's End, the greatest play of the First World War: its dugout, its officers and its ordinary courage made the war visible to the theatre audience of 1928, and it remains the most performed war play in English.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the imagist and the anti-war novel
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and biographer; one of the founders of Imagism and the author of Death of a Hero.
biography: Born Edward Godfree Aldington at Portsmouth on 8 July 1892; he was at University College London, became one of the founders of Imagism with Pound and H.D. (whom he married in 1913), and served on the Western Front from 1916. Images of War (1919), Death of a Hero (1929), the biography of Lawrence of Arabia (1955) and his later novels followed. He died at Sury-en-Vaux, France, on 27 July 1962.
literary_profile: Richard Aldington was one of the founders of Imagism and the author of Death of a Hero, the most bitterly anti-war novel of the 1929 flood: his early poems made the Imagist line, and his novel gave the war generation its most savage indictment of the war and of the society that made it.
stylistic_characteristics: The Imagist image without ornament; the free verse line of the early poems; the savage satire and the documentary detail of the novel; the first-person outburst; the refusal of consolation or rhetoric.
intellectual_concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; sexuality, the new psychology; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.
historical_significance: Richard Aldington was one of the founders of Imagism and the author of Death of a Hero: his early poems made the Imagist line, and his novel gave the war generation its most savage indictment of the war and of the society that made it.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the war poet and the composer
literary_identity: Poet and composer; the greatest English poet-composer of the century and one of the finest poets of the First World War.
biography: Born in Gloucester on 28 August 1890; he sang as a chorister at Gloucester Cathedral, studied with Charles Villiers Stanford at the Royal College of Music, and served with the Gloucestershire Regiment on the Somme, where he was gassed and wounded. Severely Poems (1917) was published in his lifetime; he was committed to mental hospitals in 1922 and died at Dartford on 26 December 1937.
literary_profile: Ivor Gurney was the greatest English poet-composer of the century and one of the finest poets of the First World War: his poems of the trenches and of Gloucestershire, written while he was confined to mental hospitals, are among the most original of the period, and his settings of English poetry are central to the English song.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, exact image of the trench and the county; the song form and the lyric refrain; the remembered landscape of Gloucestershire; the musical notation of rhythm; the direct, unornamented speech.
intellectual_concerns: The First World War and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock, mourning, and the unquiet dead; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; madness, the asylum, and the diagnosis of the will.
historical_significance: Ivor Gurney was the greatest English poet-composer of the century: his poems of the trenches and of Gloucestershire, written in mental hospitals, are among the most original of the period, and he stands with Owen and Rosenberg as one of the great poets of the war.
